clinicalPearls: Traditionally defined as dementia due primarily to one or more symptomatic strokes; ranked the second most frequent cause of dementia after Alzheimer's disease, and especially common where vascular risk factors are undertreated (p.3489).

The concept has been broadened to vascular contributions to cognitive impairment and dementia (VCID), reflecting that cerebrovascular pathology is highly prevalent in the elderly and contributes to cognitive impairment, whether in isolation or—more commonly—combined with neurodegenerative processes (p.3489).

Clinical evaluation focuses on identifying vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, atrial fibrillation, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease), prior stroke/TIA, and family history of early stroke or vascular disease (p.3491).

Although stepwise progression and deficits such as loss of executive function are particularly suggestive, most individuals with VCID follow the more typical pattern of gradual progression of impaired episodic memory (p.3491).

Patients often show a mixture of executive and visuospatial deficits with prominent psychomotor slowing, and may present with psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, delusions, disinhibition, or apathy (p.196).
Gait disturbance is common in vascular dementia (as well as PD/DLB and NPH) (p.195).

Strategic single infarcts in locations such as thalamus, medial temporal cortex, anterior corpus callosum, or dominant-side angular gyrus can sufficiently impair episodic memory and function to meet memory-based dementia criteria (p.3489).

At least some cognitive impairment is present in approximately half of stroke survivors and increases with longer follow-up; even patients with good cognitive recovery show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline (p.3489).

One late-onset community autopsy cohort attributed 25% of dementia risk to cerebrovascular disease (vs 39% Alzheimer's, 17% LATE, 12% Lewy body), and most late-onset dementia involves multiple coexisting pathologies (p.195).
harrison.pathophysiology: Vascular dementia results from the cumulative impact of cerebrovascular disease on age-related cognitive decline. Symptomatic strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic) produce irreversible injury whose cognitive effect depends on size and location. Cerebral small-vessel disease—principally arteriolosclerosis (thickening of arterioles from plasma-protein infiltration; risk factors age, hypertension, diabetes; centered on deep penetrating territories such as thalamus, basal ganglia, brainstem) and cerebral amyloid angiopathy (beta-amyloid deposition in walls of small cortical arteries/arterioles/capillaries; main risk factor advancing age; favoring lobar cortex and subcortical white matter)—is often clinically asymptomatic and produces lacunar infarcts, microinfarcts, cerebral microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities. These small distributed injuries disconnect nodes within distributed brain networks. Mixed pathology is the rule: cerebrovascular lesions frequently co-occur with neurodegenerative disease (most commonly Alzheimer's), producing greater impairment than either mechanism alone, possibly via loss of blood-brain barrier integrity and impaired perivascular clearance of beta-amyloid (p.3489-3491).
additionalDifferentials: Alzheimer's disease (most common dementia; mixed AD-vascular pathology very common)
Dementia with Lewy bodies / PDD spectrum
nonInfectiousMimics: Alzheimer's disease (frequently coexists as mixed dementia—a key pitfall)
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI is the mainstay for detection and subtyping of cerebrovascular disease; should include FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and T2*-weighted sequences to detect large and small chronic infarcts, acute microinfarcts, microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities (p.3491)
Diffusion tensor MRI (e.g., peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity, PSMD) detects white matter disconnection (largely research use) (p.3490)
Vessel imaging (CT or MR angiography) is not required for initial cognitive evaluation but may help determine the cause of identified macroscopic infarcts (p.3491)
Screening for atrial fibrillation in individuals with asymptomatic infarcts; prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic-appearing infarcts (p.3491)
Genetic testing for hereditary VCID (CADASIL, hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy) when young onset, positive family history, or suggestive imaging—otherwise unnecessary (p.3491)
redFlags: Young onset, positive family history, or suggestive neuroimaging—consider hereditary forms such as CADASIL or hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3491)
Lobar intracerebral hemorrhage or convexity subarachnoid blood, suggesting cerebral amyloid angiopathy (p.3490)
Rapid progression with motor rigidity and myoclonus suggests CJD rather than vascular dementia (p.195)
harrison.prognosis: Stroke survivors show accelerated poststroke cognitive decline even after good initial recovery; in one longitudinal study trajectory shifted from a prestroke cognitive gain to poststroke loss. Multiple strokes and larger infarcted volumes raise the likelihood of poststroke cognitive dysfunction. Epidemiologic data show declining age-adjusted dementia incidence paralleling improved hypertension control and stroke prevention, and the SPRINT-MIND trial showed intensive systolic blood pressure lowering reduced rates of mild cognitive impairment and combined MCI/probable dementia, underscoring VCID as a target for prevention (p.3489).
pitfalls: Mixed dementia is the rule rather than the exception—cerebrovascular disease commonly co-occurs with Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative pathologies, so attributing cognitive impairment to a single etiology is often incorrect (p.3489).
Most individuals with VCID do not show classic stepwise decline but instead a gradual progression of impaired episodic memory resembling Alzheimer's (p.3491).
White matter hyperintensities are an almost ubiquitous, nonspecific feature of aging (gliosis, demyelination, or increased water content) and should not be over-interpreted (p.3490).
Many chronic lacunar infarcts and microinfarcts cannot be readily identified on routine imaging, so absence of visible lesions does not exclude small-vessel disease (p.3490).
